overview.text: The Illinois Department of Transportation and the Federal Highway Administration propose to rebuild about 4.6 miles of U.S. Route 30 (Lincoln Highway) from Cicero Avenue to Chicago Road in south suburban Cook County, Illinois, widening the existing 40-foot undivided road into a divided highway — six lanes west of Western Avenue and four lanes east of it — at an estimated cost of $13.18 million. The corridor runs through the villages of Park Forest, Matteson, and Olympia Fields and the city of Chicago Heights, requiring demolition of eight buildings (six commercial, two residential), a small strip from Roosevelt Elementary School in Chicago Heights, and a 0.17-acre temporary construction easement in the 31-acre Woodrow Wilson Woods (a Cook County Forest Preserve site) to rebuild the Thorn Creek bridge. A 'no-build' option and relocating the road north or south of the existing corridor were rejected, as was a shifted-centerline 'Alignment B'; only 'Alignment A,' which keeps the road on its existing centerline, was carried to the public hearing. The main environmental impacts are predicted 1990 traffic noise levels above federal design standards at most surveyed sites (noise walls were rejected as impractical given numerous driveways), the loss of about 16 acres to right-of-way, and construction-period erosion and dust, while air quality, groundwater, and historic resources were found to be minimally affected. Public response, gathered at a June 20, 1972 hearing in Matteson and through agency review of the draft environmental statement, was generally favorable, with local officials urging prompt approval and reviewing federal and state agencies raising resolvable concerns about noise, replacement housing, and the school-property taking.

project_description.text: The Illinois Department of Transportation and FHWA propose to rebuild about 4.6 miles of U.S. Route 30 (Lincoln Highway, also designated Federal Aid Primary Route 23) from Cicero Avenue to Chicago Road in Cook County, Illinois. The existing 40-foot undivided road would become a divided highway with three 12-foot lanes each direction between Cicero and Western Avenues and two 12-foot lanes each direction from Western Avenue east to Chicago Road, with a 14–16 foot median, curb and gutter, and a closed (piped) storm drainage system. The project also replaces eight structures — including the Illinois Central Gulf Railroad underpass, the Thorn Creek bridge, two pedestrian overpasses (at Roosevelt and St. Lawrence Schools), and box culverts over Butterfield Creek, Thorn Creek, and their tributaries — and requires a 0.17-acre temporary construction easement in Woodrow Wilson Woods. Total estimated cost is $13.18 million, with a $9.23 million federal grant requested; the work is planned as five construction contracts.

affected_community.text: The corridor passes through four suburban communities south of Chicago — the villages of Park Forest, Matteson, and Olympia Fields, and the city of Chicago Heights — in Bloom and Rich Townships of Cook County, where populations more than doubled between 1950 and 1970. The four communities differ sharply in income: median family income was $11,153 in Chicago Heights, $13,951 in Park Forest, $14,045 in Matteson, and $29,781 in Olympia Fields. Eight buildings would be fully acquired — five drive-in restaurants, one office, one single-family house, and one 16-unit apartment building — affecting perhaps 30 employees. Institutional impacts include a 0.10-acre (4,385 square feet) permanent taking of frontage from the roughly three-acre Roosevelt Elementary School site in Chicago Heights (already below the commonly used five-acre minimum) and a 0.17-acre temporary easement in the 31-acre Woodrow Wilson Woods, a Cook County Forest Preserve. In Park Forest, a 20-foot right-of-way and a double row of honeysuckles planted 15 years earlier shielded homes from the highway and would be lost unless relocated.

alternatives_overview.text: Three broad categories of alternatives were considered: other travel modes, not improving the highway ('Do-Nothing'), and improving it. Rail rapid transit was rejected as unsuited to the low suburban density, and an east-west commuter rail was judged unlikely to be justified. The 'Do-Nothing' option was rejected because deteriorating pavement and rising traffic would worsen congestion, safety, noise, and air pollution. Relocating the highway north or south of the existing corridor was ruled out because it would require extensive residential takings, damage two Chicago Heights parks and two Matteson cemeteries, require relocating the Illinois Central commuter station in Olympia Fields, or take a large piece of Forest Preserve land — and the corridor is already boxed in by I-80 to the north and a proposed east-west freeway to the south. Within the existing corridor, two centerline options were studied: Alignment A, which keeps the new centerline on the existing centerline and splits takings roughly evenly, and Alignment B, which shifts the centerline to place all new right-of-way on one side; Alignment B was dropped after subdivisions built along that side eliminated its advantages. To address the taking of Roosevelt School playground land, four schemes (A–D) were developed for closing part of Sunnyside Avenue and adding it to the play area; Scheme A, providing a large cul-de-sac north of the school, was accepted.

environmental_impact.text: The most significant impact is traffic noise: predicted 1990 exterior L10 noise levels exceed the federal design standards of PPM 90-2 (70 or 75 dBA depending on land use) at most surveyed sites — 46 of 49 'Category C' sites and 26 of 28 'Category B' sites — and 10 of 28 residential interior levels would exceed the 55 dBA interior standard, but noise walls were rejected as impractical because the highway is lined with driveways that would require frequent openings in any barrier. Air quality impacts from carbon monoxide are projected to stay below the federal standards of 35 ppm (1-hour) and 9 ppm (8-hour), with a worst-case predicted concentration of 5.7 ppm. Groundwater impacts on the Silurian Dolomite Aquifer, which supplies Chicago Heights, Park Forest, Matteson, and Olympia Fields, are expected to be minor because the closed drainage system limits pollution and road-salt application rates have been reduced to 250–350 pounds per lane mile per pass. About 16.2 acres of land would be acquired and eight buildings demolished; five upsized box culverts designed for a 50-year storm should reduce upstream flooding of the kind that occurred in July 1957. No National Register historic sites, wetlands, floodplains, or important wildlife habitats are affected, and the State Historic Preservation Officer determined that no archaeological resources subject to Section 106 protection would be affected. Construction-period impacts (erosion, dust, debris) would be controlled by sodding, mulch or matting, water sprays, and a special provision limiting exposed erodible earth to 40 acres at a time.

public_response.text: A public hearing was held June 20, 1972 at the O.W. Huth Upper Grade Center in Matteson after eleven early coordination meetings between September 1970 and December 1974 with municipalities, the railroad, utilities, and the Forest Preserve District. Public response at the hearing was generally favorable, though residents raised concerns about screen plantings, signalization, business access, a possible bike path (rejected for lack of right-of-way), drainage, and street lighting. Federal reviewers had a mixed but broadly supportive response: HUD, Commerce, HEW, OEO, and the Cook County Highway Department had no objections; EPA requested more detail on noise, air quality, and solid-waste disposal; the Department of the Interior initially asked for historic-preservation consultation and stream-impact analysis and later (November 1976) had no objection to the Section 4(f) approval, concurring that there is no feasible and prudent alternative to the temporary use of Forest Preserve land. The Northeastern Illinois Planning Commission found the project consistent with regional plans but urged further attention to the Roosevelt School playground deficit. Local officials strongly supported the project: the Mayor of Chicago Heights urged prompt approval, saying the project was already behind schedule and the pavement deteriorating; the Village of Park Forest strongly supported it; and the Interstate Planning Committee voted unanimously to endorse the application.
